newsitem.title: USA: ValuJet calls for cooperative air safety effort.
newsitem.headline: ValuJet calls for cooperative air safety effort.

text.p: ValuJet chairman Lewis Jordan said Tuesday he was confident that a series of errors caused the crash of his airline's flight 592 and that a similar accident could have happened to any carrier.
He called on airlines big and small to share safety information to avoid future accidents, adding that "ValuJet volunteers to play a role. We're dedicated to that proposition."

Jordan told an aviation conference he was confident that without the series of accidents the crash of flight 592 in the Everglades near Miami last May 11, killing all 110 people on board, would not have happened.

He told the audience of aviation experts he could not pass up the chance to say "you are wrong" to think the crash of 592 could be laid to the fact Valujet was a start-up airline and it could not happened to a older carrier.
Jordan said he had studied the contract work done for both small and large carriers and the oversight given the contractors and all airlines should swap their experiences.
He said he hoped that 592 could be a catalyst for airlines to join forces to improve safety.

Atlanta-based ValuJet was put under close scrutiny by the Federal Aviation Administration after the crash and five weeks later was grounded for a series of FAA safety violations, many involving contracting work to other air services companies.
On September 26, after a series of internal reforms, ValuJet was given permission to resume a limited schedule.
Jordan said the carrier is now under close FAA scrutiny by some 60 full-time FAA inspectors, the equivalent of 600-700 inspectors looking over one of the bigger carriers.
"What we have to do as an industry together is enter a partnership where we can all learn from anything that has happened," he said.

The cause of the crash has not yet been formally ruled on by the National Transportation Safety Board, but investigators think that oxygen generators put in the plane's hold by a subcontractor may have ignited, triggering a fire.

Without saying there was any whispering campaign to cast ValuJet or smaller airlines as unsafe, Jordan said that if there is a perception that low-fare airlines by definition were unsafe, the public can be done a serious injustice.
Families might take a car over unsafe roads rather than fly on a U.S. airline, adding that "even those that have had their difficulties have an extremely high level of safety overall."
